gemini_adversarial_critique: Claude's stored row for S149 fails adversarial audit on three independent fronts: (1) obvious abstract-only numerical extraction that omits explicitly printed SEs/95% CIs and propagates an internal outcome-label swap in the paper; (2) an obsolete `reasoned non-fit` justification that contradicts the A21 synthesis-family definitions; and (3) unflagged Criterion 2 scope and data-integrity red flags requiring PI review. 1. Abstract-Only Extraction & Outcome Mislabelling: Claude copied the multi-outcome prose summary straight from the Abstract (p. 1) into `effect_estimate` and left `lower_CI`, `upper_CI`, and `standard_error` completely blank, despite Table 8 (p. 10) printing exact SEs, t-statistics, p-values, and 95% CIs for every PSM outcome. Worse, because Claude did not cross-check Results Section 3.7 (p. 9) or Table 8 (p. 10), Claude uncritically repeated the Abstract's claim that VWSC participation `"improved toilet functionality by 24.8%"`, whereas Section 3.7 and Table 8 explicitly report `+24.8%` (SE = 5.2, 95% CI [14.6%, 35.0%]) for **Water Source Functionality** and `+19.3%` (SE = 4.7, 95% CI [10.1%, 28.5%]) for **Toilet Usage Rate** (with no "toilet functionality" row in Table 8 at all). Claude also bundled a non-governance physical-geography covariate (`distance to water source`, standardized beta = 0.62 from Table 2, p. 6) and a non-Criterion 4 health outcome (`illness incidence` -12.7%) into the same string, while overlooking Table 5's (p. 8) probit marginal effect for `VWSC awareness campaign` on consistent toilet usage (+15.8 percentage points, SE = 0.047, 95% CI [0.066, 0.250]). 2. Flawed `Reasoned Non-Fit` Rationale (`questionable_could_fit_family_ABC`): Claude's `provenance_note` justifies leaving `synthesis_family` blank by citing `PROJECT_SPEC.md S8`'s narrow pre-A21 framing of Family B as strictly `"provider-side 'bureaucratic assistance' (which describes officials helping applicants navigate procedure, not citizens participating in local governance bodies)"`. Under A21, however, Family B was explicitly broadened to encompass community participation, outreach/assistance, and trust mechanisms (and Family A covers local governance arrangements). Even on Claude's own narrow provider-outreach framing, Table 5 (p. 8) directly estimates committee-led outreach (`VWSC awareness campaign` -> +15.8 pp consistent toilet usage). Thus, if S149 remains included in the review, excluding it from Family B as a `reasoned non-fit` is inconsistent with A21. 3. Narrow Criterion 2 Scope & Study-Integrity Flags (`borderline_flag_for_pi`): Applying the `2026-10-13 / 2026-10-14` CK narrow Criterion 2 standard (`A24/A26/A28`), S149 sits on a sharp eligibility knife-edge (`E03` risk). While VWSCs are formal decentralized local governance committees under India's Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission-Gramin, no legal rule, statutory mandate, gender quota, tariff, or administrative eligibility rule varies across the 16 sampled villages in Odisha (mandating 50% women's representation in VWSCs is proposed only as a future policy recommendation in Section 4.5b, p. 14). Instead, the empirical exposure is a behavioural/empowerment composite (`Women's Agency Score 0-10`: attendance 20%, speaking time 30%, decision influence 30%, leadership 20%; p. 4) binarized at an unstated cutoff. Moreover, the paper exhibits severe reporting/validity defects: every mathematical equation in Sections 2.4-2.6 (pp. 3-5) failed to render in the published PDF (`disp lay-eq- Equa`, `inli ne-eq-IEq1`), the PSM analysis treats village-level VWSC participation across just 16 villages (400 households) without reporting the propensity model, matched N, balance diagnostics, or village-cluster inference, and the Abstract/Conclusion contradict Table 8 on which WASH facility improved by 24.8%. The PI should determine whether de facto VWSC participation / awareness campaigns pass narrow Criterion 2 (in which case S149 belongs in Family B with corrected Table 8/Table 5 statistics) or fail under `E03`/quality screening.

phase1_headline_summary: Primary headline estimate (2017 survey, Table 6, PDF p. 10; Abstract p. 1; text pp. 8, 10): Household in a community with Water Safety Plan programming (`WSP = 1` vs. `0`) predicting household drinking-water free chlorine residual > 0.1 mg/L (`FCR_Bin`): mixed-effect logistic regression `mOR = 24.16` (`95% CI: 5.93–98.48` in Table 6; rounded to `5.93–98.5` in Abstract/text; `p < 0.05`, SE and exact p-value not reported), adjusting for significant multivariate predictors (`MixedWater`, `MainSource`, `Handwashing`, `SeparateWater`, `AdequateWater`, `Shelter`, `WasteDisposal`) and sub-district random effects; corresponding unadjusted `OR = 6.7` (`2.71–16.57` in Table 6; `6.70, 2.70–16.57` in text p. 8) and multivariate adjusted `aOR = 9.75` (`95% CI: 6.85–14.05`, `p < 0.05`). Secondary estimates in Table 6 (2017 `FCR > 0.1 mg/L`): `MainSource` (piped network = 1 vs. private trucked water = 0) flips sign from `uOR = 1.59 (95% CI: 1.23–2.05)` to `aOR = 0.47 (95% CI: 0.31–0.72, p < 0.05)` and `mOR = 0.56 (95% CI: 0.34–0.92, p < 0.05)` (piped network associated with lower odds of chlorinated water than trucked water); `MixedWater` `mOR = 2.11 (95% CI: 1.34–3.32, p < 0.05)`; `Handwashing` `mOR = 1.80 (95% CI: 1.26–2.57, p < 0.05)`; `Displacement` (IDP = 1 vs. permanent resident = 0) `uOR = 0.92 (95% CI: 0.81–1.05, NS)`. Childhood diarrhea (<5 years, past 2 weeks) regressions (Tables 4–5, PDF pp. 9–10): `WSP` adjusted NS in 2016 (`aOR = 1.03, 95% CI: 0.75–1.40`) and 2017 (`aOR = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.58–1.17`); `Displacement` adjusted NS in 2016 (`aOR = 1.26, 95% CI: 0.95–1.67`) and unadjusted NS in 2017 (`uOR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.85–1.17`) (note: p. 7 text transposes the Table 4 mixed-effect ORs for `SeparateWater` [2.11] and `AdequateWater` [2.04]). Descriptive 2016 vs. 2017 two-sample t-tests (Tables 1–2, PDF pp. 4, 8): piped network as main source declined from `22.0%` (`282/1281`) to `15.3%` (`208/1360`, `p < 0.001`), private water trucking rose from `77.0%` (`986/1281`) to `82.5%` (`1122/1360`, `p < 0.001`), mean share of income spent on water rose from `20.5% (SD 13.1)` to `21.9% (SD 15.4)` (`p < 0.001`), and `FCR > 0.1 mg/L` rose from `4.1%` (`52/1281`) to `27.9%` (`380/1360`, `p < 0.001`).
claude_effect_estimate: Free chlorine residual (FCR) >0.1 mg/L increased from 4.1% to 27.9% (2016-2017), strongly associated with WSP programming (mOR 24.16, 95% CI 5.93-98.5); piped water as main source declined 22.0% to 15.3%; childhood diarrhea prevalence declined 32.8% to 20.4%.

However, there is a sample-size and comparator discrepancy on the headline regression: `sample_size` lists `"1281 (2016) + 1360 (2017) household surveys"` and `comparator_definition` states `"pre-WSP baseline, 2016"`, whereas 2016 FCR regressions were not estimated (PDF p. 8), 35.4% (453/1,281) of 2016 households already had WSP programming (Table 1), and `mOR = 24.16` in Table 6 was estimated solely on the 2017 cross-section (`N = 1,360` households with children <5, out of 1,921 total 2017 surveys; `n = 1,344` with measured FCR; complete-case regression N not separately printed), adjusting for `MixedWater`, `MainSource`, `Handwashing`, `SeparateWater`, `AdequateWater`, `Shelter`, `WasteDisposal`, and sub-district random effects.
gemini_adversarial_critique: Adversarial audit of S178 (Sikder et al. 2018, Conflict and Health) uncovers two substantive defects in Claude's stored `effect_sizes.csv` row alongside a review-level eligibility failure under the narrow Criterion 2 / conflict-scope standard. 1. Mischaracterization of regression sample, wave structure, and comparator: Claude records `sample_size = "1281 (2016) + 1360 (2017) household surveys"`, `exposure_definition = "...compared across repeated cross-sectional survey waves (2016 vs. 2017)"`, and `comparator_definition = "Survey wave/area without WSP programming in place (pre-WSP baseline, 2016)"`. In the paper, although descriptive prevalence shifts (FCR > 0.1 mg/L rising from 4.1% to 27.9%; piped network declining from 22.0% to 15.3%; childhood diarrhea declining from 32.8% to 20.4%) compare the 2016 (N = 1,281) and 2017 (N = 1,360) analytic samples of households with children <5, 2016 was NOT a pre-WSP baseline—35.4% (453/1,281) of 2016 households were already in WSP communities (Table 1, PDF p. 4)—and 2016 FCR regressions were omitted altogether due to low FCR concentrations (PDF p. 8). The headline mixed-effect odds ratio (`mOR = 24.16`, `95% CI: 5.93–98.48` in Table 6; rounded to `5.93–98.5` in Abstract/text) was estimated exclusively within the 2017 cross-section (`N = 1,360` households with children <5; `n = 1,344` with measured FCR in Table 2), comparing `WSP = 1` (41.3%, 562 households) against `WSP = 0` communities in 2017. 2. Mischaracterization of WSP as a legal/regulatory enforcement mechanism (Criterion 2 `E03` and conflict scope `E05`): Claude labels WSP `"water-quality regulatory programming (an enforcement/regulatory mechanism)"` and `"water-quality regulatory compliance"`. Full-text inspection shows that vendors operated in `"unregulated environments"` (PDF p. 11) in opposition-controlled southern Syria during active armed conflict; regulation and targeted subsidies appear only as normative policy recommendations in the Abstract, Discussion, and Conclusions. Empirically, `WSP` was a UNICEF/NGO Whole-of-Syria WASH Cluster emergency operational package comprising risk assessments, chlorination training, distribution of chlorine and pooltesters, well chlorination stations, volunteer household water-safety awareness campaigns, and physical repair of water lines and pumps (PDF pp. 2, 11). Under the `CK` narrow Criterion 2 standard applied in `A24/A26/A28` (excluding non-legal engineering/operational WASH interventions), S178 fails narrow Criterion 2 (`E03`) and sits in an active armed-conflict humanitarian relief setting (`E05`), rendering SWiM family placement moot (though even if retained, keeping it out of Families A–C as a non-fit would be fully justified).

Two minor descriptive inaccuracies appear in `effect_sizes.csv` metadata: (1) `adjusted` lists `source` and `race/ethnicity` among the covariates in the MR model, whereas LASSO dropped `Source`, `%Hispanic or Latino` (the sole ethnicity variable), `%Black`, and `%Asian` from the final MR specification while retaining `%American Indian or Alaska Native`, `%Native Hawaii or Pacific Islander`, and the `%Homeownership x %Native Hawaii or Pacific Islander` interaction (Section 2.4, p. 5; Table 1, p. 6); and (2) `effect_measure` repeats the authors' own terminology ('adjusted odds ratio (OR)') for exponentiated negative-binomial regression coefficients on active-year-normalized violation counts, which are technically incidence/rate ratios. gemini_adversarial_critique: 1. SCOPE & ELIGIBILITY AUDIT (E03 / E05 UNDER A24/A26/A28 STANDARD): Marcillo, Krometis, and Krometis (2021) is an ecological environmental-justice geospatial study asking whether SDWA violation counts across N = 662 geocoded Virginia community water systems (CWSs) vary by zip-code racial/ethnic composition, rurality, and Census homeownership (explicitly used solely as an area-level wealth/SES proxy because 2000 zip-code Census files lacked income and education, p. 4). As Claude's own `effect_estimate` note concedes in referencing excluded study S135, the paper's primary headline exposure (%Black on Health-Based [HB] violations, OR = 1.031) fails narrow Criterion 2 because population demographic composition is not a legal or administrative exposure (E03). To salvage an institutional row under the one-effect-per-study rule, `effect_sizes.csv` extracted a system-level control covariate—binary utility ownership (`Operation: Private` vs. `Public`)—predicting Monitoring & Reporting (`MR`) violations (OR = 1.899). Under the strict 2026-10-13/14 CK standard (`A24/A26/A28`, which excluded non-legal exposures and non-household administrative outcomes like building permits in S1121), this row still fails both narrow Criterion 2 (`E03`) and Criterion 4 (`E05`): (a) on Criterion 2, binary private vs. public utility ownership is a macro provider-ownership attribute, not a last-mile legal/administrative rule governing household service access (the authors themselves caution on p. 7 that the binary public/private indicator does not capture institutional governance differences); and (b) on Criterion 4, `MR` violations measure a utility's administrative failure to test water or file monitoring reports with the state/EPA primacy agency (p. 3)—a regulator-facing utility paperwork/testing compliance count, not household water connection, continuity, affordability, or tap water quality. Moreover, unconnected private-well households and historical boundary/redlining exclusions from CWS service are omitted by design (pp. 3, 8). 2. OUTCOME-CHOICE & DIRECTION AUDIT IF RETAINED: Coding `MR` paperwork/reporting violations under `outcome_family = effective_access` conflates administrative reporting non-compliance with safe drinking-water delivery; the paper's actual water-quality compliance outcome is `HB` violations (MCL/MRDL/treatment-technique breaches), for which `Private vs. Public` ownership was statistically null (OR = 1.425, 95% CI: 0.837, 2.428; Table 1, p. 6). Furthermore, `direction = positive` in `effect_sizes.csv` reflects the raw regression sign (`OR > 1`, more violations) rather than improved household access (higher MR violation odds = worse utility regulatory compliance). 3. NON-FIT VERDICT CONDITIONAL ON RETENTION: Because the study appears likely ineligible (`E03`/`E05`), family assignment is moot (`moot_study_appears_ineligible`). However, if the PI elects to retain S353 as a borderline regulatory-regime study, leaving `synthesis_family` blank (`reasoned non-fit`) is fully justified: provider ownership structure (`Private` vs. `Public` CWS) predicting SDWA regulator reporting violations does not fit Family A (household property/tenure recognition), Family B (bureaucratic assistance/facilitation), or Family C (household-facing administrative/documentation/fee barriers).

(2) Wastewater coverage (WWC, % served population, Table 5, PDF p. 6, baseline OLS FE preferred by Mundlak test = 18.460, p < 0.01): IMC binary participation β = −2.311 (SE = 2.189, p >= 0.10, null); IMCd duration β = +0.880* (SE = 0.485, p < 0.10, favorable access direction: +0.880 percentage points per year; FGLS RE β = +0.569, SE = 0.375, ns). gemini_adversarial_critique: 1. Non-fit classification (`justified_nonfit`): CK's A26 ruling (2026-10-14) moving S606 out of Family C to reasoned non-fits is completely justified. Conceptually, China's `hukou` registration institution relates to legal residency status (adjacent to Family A, not Family C), not utility governance or decentralized service delivery. Empirically, however, neither the ecological city-level predictor (`Temporary residents (%)`) nor the outcome (bulk municipal wastewater treatment plant capacity/throughput per 10,000 persons) is construct-compatible with Family A household or settlement legal-recognition/tenure effects on household WASH access. Note on directionality: the raw sign is negative (beta = -0.00164), meaning a higher share of legally unrecognized temporary migrants is associated with lower per-capita wastewater plant capacity (substantively, legal exclusion harms infrastructure supply). 2. Review eligibility & hidden scope vulnerabilities (`borderline_flag_for_pi` for E03/E04): Unlike excluded studies with wholly non-WASH outcomes (e.g., building permits S1121) or wholly non-legal exposures (e.g., social trust S1144, watershed engineering S1020), S606 retains a borderline link to municipal sanitation infrastructure (wastewater treatment) and an official public-security registration category (`hukou` vs. temporary resident registration), explaining why CK kept it as a reasoned non-fit in A26. However, full-text audit reveals that Claude's stored row materially overstated scope fit on both criteria: - Narrow Criterion 2 (`E03` risk): Claude's provenance note calls this "A clean legal/administrative-status exposure (hukou household registration)", omitting that the authors deliberately restricted the panel to 2008-2014 to avoid China's 2014 national `hukou` policy reform (p. 784) and measured zero city-level variation in `hukou` eligibility rules or quotas. Instead, the predictor is aggregate city demographic composition (`Temporary residents (%)`), which the authors acknowledge in their limitations (p. 790) cannot isolate planning/governance mechanisms. - Criterion 4 (`E04` risk & mislabeled `outcome_family`): Claude coded `outcome_family = "service_coverage"` and mingled non-WASH municipal solid-waste capacity (tons/day) and public green space into `effect_estimate` and `standard_error`. In the paper, the two WASH-related metrics measure back-end municipal sewage treatment plant capacity and treated volume per 10,000 population, and the authors explicitly concede (p. 785) that limited information precludes ascertaining whether the local population directly benefits from pollutant treatment plant construction. Numerical & Packaging Audit: Every printed number in Claude's `effect_sizes.csv` row matches Lewis (2014) verbatim across pp. 417, 420, 425, 427 (Table 7), 429, and 430 (Table 10). However, the `effect_estimate` cell packages a multi-stage composite rather than a single clean treatment effect: it combines (a) a two-part hurdle-model marginal effect on an institutional/fiscal intermediate input (`739.1` constant-2000 Rp/capita PDAM equity investment, `z = 3.20`, Table 7), (b) per-Rupiah capital-spending semi-elasticities on household connections (`0.0003, t = 6.16` exogenous; `0.0004, t = 1.71` endogenous, Table 10), and (c) derived marginal unit costs (`Rp 2.5-2.9M` vs `Rp 6.9-8.2M`). Three reporting nuances warrant note: (i) the Table 10 outcome is the *log* of new household connections per 1,000 persons (Claude's prose omits `log`, likely echoing p. 429 prose and Table 10's own misprinted footnote that erroneously labels the DV as equity investment); (ii) the preferred endogenous slope `0.0004 (t = 1.71)` is only marginally significant at `* p < 0.10`, not `p < 0.05`; and (iii) Claude's `provenance_note` praises the endogenous-transfer instrumentation as "well-identified", whereas the excluded instruments (an on/off-Java location dummy and a year dummy, p. 424) very plausibly violate the exclusion restriction with respect to municipal utility connection growth. 2. Justification of SWiM Non-Fit (`justified_nonfit`): Leaving `synthesis_family` blank is strongly justified even under broadened A21 family labels. First, Lewis never estimates the total (reduced-form) effect of Water Hibah program participation on household water connections: every connection regression (Tables 8-10) conditions on PDAM equity investment per capita—the exact causal mediator through which WH operates—rendering the binary WH dummy a mediator-blocked direct residual (`0.3816, t = 1.58` in Table 8 endogenous; `0.2892, t = 1.04` in Table 10 endogenous). Second, the statistically significant Table 10 predictors are continuous fiscal-expenditure slopes per constant-2000 Rupiah per capita rather than legal/institutional rule effects. Third, substantively, an intergovernmental performance grant reimbursing municipal utility capital outlays does not cleanly fit Family A (legal recognition/tenure/eligibility), Family B (household-facing bureaucratic/procedural facilitation), or Family C (legal/administrative barriers). 3. Review Scope / Eligibility (`borderline_flag_for_pi`): While Criterion 4 is clearly met in Tables 8-10 (`log of number of new household connections per 1,000 people`; note P2D2 in Tables 3-4 and WH Tables 5-7 do not measure household access), S636 is a textbook borderline Criterion 2 case warranting PI review against `E03` (financial/capital subsidy without a legal/administrative access rule). Water Hibah reimburses ~45% of connection capital costs (`Rp 2-3 million` per connection, p. 417, p. 431) without altering household tenure, customer eligibility law, documentation hurdles, or disconnection rules, and Footnote 6 (p. 418) notes data cannot verify whether connections reached poor households. Conversely, because WH codifies formal Ministry of Finance intergovernmental conditional-transfer, mandatory municipal matching-equity, and independent operational-verification rules, it sits right on the boundary between an `E03` capital grant and an administrative service-delivery governance rule.

gemini_adversarial_critique: Three substantive issues emerge from auditing S869 against the full text: 1. CRITICAL SIGN / DIRECTION INVERSION IN `effect_sizes.csv`: Claude defines the exposure as consortium cooperation (`Cooperation = 1`) and the comparator as stand-alone municipal provision (`Cooperation = 0`), then records `direction = "null for water coverage (not significant); positive and significant for sewage coverage"` based on `B = .466 (p = .007)` in Table 4 (PDF p. 6). However, SPSS GLM sets the highest category (`Cooperation = 1`) as the reference group and explicitly labels the Table 4 row `Cooperation = 0`. Thus `B = +0.466` means *non-cooperating* (`Cooperation = 0`) municipalities have higher log sewage coverage than cooperating (`Cooperation = 1`) municipalities—i.e., the coefficient for consortium cooperation (`Cooperation = 1` vs `0`) is NEGATIVE (`B = -0.466`), matching both the prose on PDF p. 6 ("the total population served by sewage services decreased when local government units cooperated (M = 52,0) against those units that did not cooperate (M = 57,0)") and the subgroup means Claude itself pasted (`M = 41.58` cooperating vs `M = 59.45` non-cooperating). In addition, Table 4 includes three uncentered interaction terms (`Cooperation = 0 * invest water`, `Cooperation = 0 * invest sewage`, `Cooperation = 0 * contract management`), so `B = 0.466` is only a conditional intercept shift at zero log-investment, whereas the negative interaction `Cooperation = 0 * invest sewage` (`B = -0.081, p = .021`) indicates that sewage capital investment translates more strongly into sewage coverage inside consortia (`B = 0.123, p = .001`). Leaving `direction` as "positive and significant for sewage coverage" inverts the paper's empirical finding. 2. QUESTIONABLE SWiM NON-FIT (`Family C` CANDIDATE): While `included_in_pooled_estimate = FALSE` is completely appropriate (observational panel GLM with uncentered interactions, log10-transformed SNIS index outcomes, and explicit reverse causality), leaving `synthesis_family` blank as a `reasoned non-fit` is questionable. Claude's rationale conflates meta-analytic poolability (whether a second study shares the exact Brazilian consortium GLM operationalization) with SWiM narrative/direction family assignment. Under the broadened Family C definition (ownership, regulation, decentralization, institutional capacity, and utility governance/contracting structures), delegating municipal water/wastewater planning, regulation, and delivery to a statutory intermunicipal public consortium via a `program contract` versus stand-alone municipal provision maps directly onto `Family C`—provided the sign inversion and reverse-causality caveat are corrected first. 3. BORDERLINE NARROW CRITERION 2 SCOPE (`borderline_flag_for_pi`): Unlike excluded non-legal exposure studies (e.g., watershed engineering or social trust) or fiscal-only consortium studies (`S837`), S869 does examine a formal legal-institutional mechanism—municipal entry into a public sanitation consortium under Brazil's 2007 Federal Sanitation Guidelines and 2020 Sanitation Legal Framework Act, which requires city council legislative approval and a binding `program contract`—paired with genuine municipal water and sewage population-coverage outcomes (Criterion 4). Nevertheless, under the strict `CK` narrow Criterion 2 standard, intermunicipal utility consolidation/contracting is an upstream public-administration governance structure rather than a household-facing legal rule governing last-mile access (and the paper's co-focal 'transaction cost' variables are capital-investment spending [`E03`] and single- vs dual-service operation). Combined with severe selection/reverse causality acknowledged by the authors (small municipalities with <50,000 residents join consortia *because* baseline sewage coverage is low), S869 warrants `borderline_flag_for_pi` review.

Statistical & Factual Audit of Stored Row: Every numerical value in `effect_sizes.csv` (`OR = 4.27`, `95% CI: 3.07–5.93`, blank `standard_error`, regression `n = 938`, descriptive `N = 1,021` with `487` POS and `534` non-POS, and unadjusted `OR = 7.225, 95% CI: 5.389–9.686` in `provenance_note`) matches Sarfo (2025) exactly. In Portage County, the binding legal rule that differs by context is narrower: under OAC Chapter 3701-29, PCHD allows incremental repairs for owner-occupied non-POS failures while disallowing incremental repairs for POS failures (PDF p. 95 / diss. p. 78), alongside equal 60+60-day BOH NOV enforcement across all failed systems. 2. Critique of `reasoned non-fit` Classification: Leaving `synthesis_family` blank (`justified_nonfit`) is methodologically sound even under the broadened A21 Family C definition (regulation, enforcement & oversight). All 938 analytic units are existing household septic systems that failed inspection and received the identical 60+60-day BOH NOV enforcement citation; the predictor contrasts real-estate transfer context (voluntary POS) against routine/complaint/stormwater inspection triggers, and the dependent variable is strictly administrative abatement speed (`<=120` days vs. `>120` days). Crucially, connecting a home with a failed septic tank to a public sanitary sewer—a superior household sanitation upgrade—strongly *reduces* 120-day NOV compliance (`adjusted OR = 0.33`, `95% CI: 0.14–0.81`, `p = 0.02`; text `OR = 0.332`, `p = 0.0153`) because municipal sewer permitting and construction exceed 120 days. Pooling 120-day NOV deadline compliance into Family C as a positive sanitation-access/service-quality effect would invert substantive WASH upgrades and conflate transactional urgency with service access. Grouping S331 with S178 (Water Safety Plan compliance) and S353 (SDWA violations) as non-pooled `administrative_outcome` rows is internally consistent. 3. Scope Audit (Narrow Criterion 2 & Criterion 4 under A24/A26/A28 Standards): Although S331 was retained under open item A13, it sits squarely on the review's eligibility boundary (`borderline_flag_for_pi`). First, under narrow Criterion 2, because Portage County's POS program is voluntary and does not legally block title transfer (unlike mandatory transfer-blocking laws in Summit/Stark counties or Iowa/Massachusetts), the POS vs. non-POS contrast primarily captures private real-estate market, lender, and escrow leverage interacting with a routine inspection service (PDF p. 97 / diss. p. 80), with only a secondary administrative rule difference (no incremental repairs at POS). Second, under Criterion 4, the study measures homeowner timeliness in abating an environmental/public-health effluent violation (`<=120` days) among homes that already possess sanitation infrastructure, rather than household water/sanitation connection, coverage, affordability, or service access—placing it very close to `E04` (environmental pollution-control / regulatory-deadline compliance) and non-household administrative outcomes excluded in A24/A26/A28 (e.g., `S1121`). If retained in the review, `exposure_definition` should be corrected to state that Portage County's POS inspection is a voluntary county service rather than a mandatory transfer requirement.
